title: Each returns to its root
hook: reach utmost emptiness, hold to stillness; all things return to their root (Tao Te Ching 16)
carry: returning to the root is stillness

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was muddy water: you can't stir it clear, but left still, it clears. Your line was let it settle.

Down, in, quieter, emptier. Lay this week's chapters side by side and that's the direction they keep pointing: a cup not filled to the brim, a soft breath like a sleeping baby's, the hole in a wheel's hub, too many colors and a numb eye, praise and blame both startling, something you look for and can't see, a jar of muddy water set down to clear. Chapter sixteen of the Tao Te Ching, today's chapter, names where that direction leads. It calls it the root.
screen: `SOFT BREATH. THE EMPTY CENTER. LESS TO SEE.` → `FAVOR AND DISGRACE. CAN'T BE SEEN. LET IT SETTLE.` → `DOWN, IN, QUIETER.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. The chapter opens by asking for emptiness taken as far as it goes, and stillness held steadily. Not a picture this time, but something close to a method: empty out, and keep still. Second, what you see from there. From that stillness, you watch all things rise and watch them return. Things grow and flourish, and each goes back to its root. A leaf comes out in spring and falls in autumn. A thought appears and fades. A wave lifts and sinks back into the sea. The rising is real. So is the going back. Third, the chain. Then a short ladder. Returning to the root is stillness. Stillness is going back to what you're meant to be. That is the constant. Knowing the constant is called clear seeing. Not knowing it, the chapter warns, people act blindly and bring trouble on themselves. Each step leans on the one before, so it's worth reading slowly. Fourth, comfort as well as teaching. Whoever knows the constant, the chapter ends, becomes open, and from openness comes fairness, and so on, step by step, up to the Tao, which lasts. To the end of one's life, it says, there is no danger. Some readers hear reassurance as much as instruction. Things go back where they came from. You don't have to drag yourself there. You return.
screen: `EMPTINESS AS FAR AS IT GOES.` · `ALL THINGS RISE, AND RETURN.` · `THE ROOT IS STILLNESS.` · `KNOWING THE CONSTANT IS CLEAR SEEING.` · then, large: `EACH RETURNS TO ITS ROOT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be soft, the way it was on the first day of this week, and watch what rises: a sound, a thought, an itch, a memory. Don't follow it out; watch it come up and sink back, the way a wave returns to the sea. Each time you notice you've wandered, that noticing is the return, so come back to the stillness and rest there.
Return to the root. Chapter sixteen's picture: everything that rises goes back where it came from, and that going back is stillness. Today's word.
Your line: returning to the root is stillness. Whatever rises goes back where it came from. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter sixteen as a guide to sitting still: they watch thoughts and sensations rise and fall away, and keep coming back to the quiet beneath them.

notes: Chapter 16 paraphrased throughout. 'Going back to what you're meant to be' renders 復命 (return to one's destiny / mandate), and 'clear seeing' renders 明; translations differ. Confirm.

The chapter's final chain (knowing the constant leads to openness, impartiality, kingliness, heaven, the Tao, and lasting without danger to the end of the body) is compressed; confirm the compression is fair.
'For some readers it lands as a reassurance' is an unsourced 'many' claim; consider 'for some readers'.
